## Azure Infrastructure Blog

### Deploying an AI Application on Azure Container Apps

- **Link**: [https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/azure-infrastructure-blog/deploying-an-ai-application-on-azure-container-apps/ba-p/4572612](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/azure-infrastructure-blog/deploying-an-ai-application-on-azure-container-apps/ba-p/4572612)
- **Published**: 2026-11-12 04:12:23
- **Fetched**: 2026-11-12 22:22:30

<details class="entry-summary">
<summary>詳細を表示</summary>
<p>AI applications often start as prototypes running locally on a developer’s machine. A Streamlit application may work perfectly in a development environment, but making it accessible to users introduces a different set of infrastructure and operational considerations.</p>
<p>From an infrastructure engineer’s perspective, the key questions are:</p>
<ul>
<li>How do we package the application?</li>
<li>Where do we store and manage container images?</li>
<li>How do we securely manage API keys and secrets?</li>
<li>How do we expose the application to users?</li>
<li>How do we scale it as usage increases?</li>
<li>How do we automate deployments and future releases?</li>
<li>How do we monitor and troubleshoot the application after deployment?</li>
</ul>
<p>This article walks through the end-to-end deployment lifecycle of an AI application using <strong>Azure Container Apps (ACA)</strong>, focusing on infrastructure, security, deployment and operational responsibilities rather than application development.</p>
<h2>1. Understanding the Architecture</h2>
<p>Before starting the deployment, it is important to understand how the different components fit together.</p>
<p>At a high level, the deployment follows this flow:</p>
<p><strong>Application Source Code → Container Image → Azure Container Registry → Azure Container Apps → Azure OpenAI</strong></p>
<p>Additional Azure services provide identity, security, networking and operational capabilities around the application.</p>
<h3>High-level architecture</h3>
<img />
<p>The responsibilities of the major components are:</p>
<div class="styles_lia-table-wrapper__h6Xo9 styles_table-responsive__MW0lN"><table border="1" style="border-width: 1px;"><tbody><tr><th>Azure component</th><th>Purpose</th></tr><tr><td>Azure Container Registry (ACR)</td><td>Stores and manages container images</td></tr><tr><td>Azure Container Apps Environment</td><td>Provides the managed environment for container applications</td></tr><tr><td>Azure Container Apps</td><td>Hosts and runs the application containers</td></tr><tr><td>Microsoft Entra ID</td><td>Provides identity and authentication</td></tr><tr><td>Managed Identity</td><td>Enables passwordless access to supported Azure services</td></tr><tr><td>Azure Key Vault</td><td>Securely stores application secrets</td></tr><tr><td>Azure Monitor</td><td>Provides monitoring and metrics</td></tr><tr><td>Log Analytics</td><td>Stores and supports analysis of application and platform logs</td></tr><tr><td>Azure OpenAI</td><td>Provides AI model inference capabilities</td></tr></tbody><colgroup><col style="width: 50.00%;" /><col style="width: 50.00%;" /></colgroup></table></div>
<p>The overall infrastructure lifecycle can be summarized as:</p>
<p><strong>Package → Build → Registry → Deploy → Secure → Scale → Automate → Monitor</strong></p>
<h2>2. Start with a Clear Application Handoff</h2>
<p>As an infrastructure engineer, I should not need to redesign the application before deploying it.</p>
<p>The application team should provide a deployment-ready application package with the following information:</p>
<ul>
<li>Application source code</li>
<li>Dockerfile</li>
<li>Dependency file, such as requirements.txt</li>
<li>Application listening port</li>
<li>Required environment variables</li>
<li>External service endpoints</li>
<li>Health-check requirements</li>
<li>Expected CPU and memory requirements</li>
<li>Authentication and integration requirements</li>
</ul>
<p>For example, a Streamlit application commonly uses port 8501.</p>
<p>It is important to establish clear ownership between the teams.</p>
<p><strong>Application team responsibilities:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Application functionality and business logic</li>
<li>Application dependencies</li>
<li>Application-level configuration</li>
<li>Application testing</li>
<li>Application-level troubleshooting</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Infrastructure team responsibilities:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Container build infrastructure</li>
<li>Container registry</li>
<li>Azure resource provisioning</li>
<li>Identity and access management</li>
<li>Secrets management</li>
<li>Networking and ingress</li>
<li>Application deployment</li>
<li>Scaling and monitoring</li>
<li>CI/CD infrastructure</li>
</ul>
<p>This separation prevents an infrastructure deployment activity from unintentionally becoming an application development task.</p>
<h2>3. Containerize the Application</h2>
<p>Before deploying an application to Azure Container Apps, we need to package it as a container image.</p>
<p>The Dockerfile defines how the application is packaged, including its base image, dependencies, working directory and startup command.</p>
<p>From an infrastructure perspective, the following items should be validated:</p>
<ol>
<li>Is the expected base image being used?</li>
<li>Are application dependencies installed successfully?</li>
<li>Is the correct application port configured?</li>
<li>Does the application listen on 0.0.0.0 rather than only localhost?</li>
<li>Is the container configured to run as a non-root user wherever possible?</li>
<li>Are sensitive files and credentials excluded from the image?</li>
</ol>
<p>For example, build and test the container locally:</p>
<p><strong>Build the image:</strong></p>
<p>docker build -t ai-app:v1 .</p>
<p><strong>Run the container:</strong></p>
<p>docker run -p 8501:8501 ai-app:v1</p>
<p>Podman can also be used in environments where Docker is unavailable or not permitted.</p>
<p>For a Streamlit application, ensure that the application startup configuration listens on all interfaces:</p>
<p>streamlit run app.py --server.address=0.0.0.0 --server.port=8501</p>
<p>Before introducing Azure into the troubleshooting process, validate that the container starts and the application is accessible locally.</p>
<p>The objective at this stage is simple:</p>
<p><strong>Can the application run successfully as a container?</strong></p>
<p>If not, resolve the container or application startup issue first. Introducing Azure Container Apps at this point adds another troubleshooting layer.</p>
<h2>4. Store the Container Image in Azure Container Registry</h2>
<p>Once the container image has been validated, it needs to be stored in a registry that Azure Container Apps can access.</p>
<p>For an Azure-native deployment, <strong>Azure Container Registry (ACR)</strong> is a suitable option.</p>
<p>The deployment flow now becomes:</p>
<p><strong>Application Code → Build Container → Test Container → Push Image to ACR → Deploy to Azure Container Apps</strong></p>
<p>One convenient option is to build the image directly using ACR.</p>
<p>az acr build \ --registry &lt;ACR_NAME&gt; \ --image ai-app:v1 \ .</p>
<p>This command builds the image from the current directory and pushes it to the specified Azure Container Registry.</p>
<p>For production deployments, avoid relying exclusively on a mutable tag such as latest.</p>
<p>Prefer traceable image versions:</p>
<p>ai-app:v1 ai-app:v2 ai-app:v3</p>
<p>For automated deployments, the image can also be tagged using a source commit ID or build number.</p>
<p>For example:</p>
<p>ai-app:build-1025</p>
<p>The complete image reference will look like:</p>
<p>&lt;ACR_NAME&gt;.azurecr.io/ai-app:v1</p>
<p>This makes it easier to identify which application version is deployed and simplifies rollback and troubleshooting.</p>
<p><strong>Infrastructure consideration:</strong> Ensure that Azure Container Apps has the appropriate permissions to pull images from the private registry. Managed identity with the required ACR permissions can be used instead of maintaining registry credentials.</p>
<h2>5. Deploy the Application to Azure Container Apps</h2>
<p>Once the container image is available in ACR, the next step is deploying it to Azure Container Apps.</p>
<p>Two important concepts need to be understood.</p>
<h3>Azure Container Apps Environment</h3>
<p>The Container Apps Environment provides the managed hosting boundary for container applications.</p>
<p>It provides shared capabilities such as networking, logging and integration with the underlying managed platform.</p>
<p>Multiple container apps can run within the same environment.</p>
<h3>Azure Container App</h3>
<p>The Container App represents the actual application deployment.</p>
<p>It contains the configuration required to run the workload, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>Container image and version</li>
<li>CPU and memory allocation</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>Ingress configuration</li>
<li>Target application port</li>
<li>Secrets</li>
<li>Scaling configuration</li>
<li>Health probes</li>
</ul>
<p>The deployment structure can be visualized as:</p>
<img />
<p>For a Streamlit application, the Container Apps target port should match the port on which the application listens inside the container.</p>
<p>At this stage, the infrastructure team owns the hosting configuration while the application code remains within the application team's ownership.</p>
<h2>6. Secure Application Secrets</h2>
<p>This is one of the most important considerations when deploying AI applications.</p>
<p>AI applications frequently require credentials to access Azure OpenAI, external APIs or other services.</p>
<p>A simple rule should always be followed:</p>
<p><strong>Never store production API keys or credentials inside application source code or container images.</strong></p>
<p>Avoid hardcoded credentials:</p>
<p>API_KEY = "xxxxxxxx"</p>
<p>Production credentials should also not be committed to source repositories through .env files.</p>
<p>There are three important approaches to consider.</p>
<h3>Option 1: Managed Identity</h3>
<p>Where the target Azure service supports Microsoft Entra authentication, use Managed Identity instead of storing application credentials.</p>
<p>For example, an application can authenticate to supported Azure services using its assigned identity.</p>
<h3>Option 2: Azure Key Vault</h3>
<p>When an application requires a secret, such as an API key or connection string, store it centrally in Azure Key Vault.</p>
<p>Access should be controlled through Managed Identity and appropriate RBAC permissions.</p>
<h3>Option 3: Azure Container Apps Secrets</h3>
<p>Azure Container Apps supports application-level secrets that can be referenced by container environment variables or mounted as files.</p>
<p>It can also reference secrets stored in Azure Key Vault using Managed Identity.</p>
<p>A recommended secret-management flow is:</p>
<img />
<p>The objective is to minimize the number of long-lived credentials that application and infrastructure teams need to manage.</p>
<h2>7. Configure Managed Identity</h2>
<p>Managed Identity helps reduce credential-management overhead and eliminates the need to maintain application credentials for supported Azure integrations.</p>
<p>For example, the access pattern can look like this:</p>
<img />
<p>Instead of storing a service principal password or application credential, the application uses its assigned identity to authenticate.</p>
<p>For Azure OpenAI, assign the appropriate role, such as <strong>Cognitive Services OpenAI User</strong>, when using Microsoft Entra authentication.</p>
<p>For Key Vault, assign <strong>Key Vault Secrets User</strong> when the application identity needs to retrieve secrets.</p>
<p>The exact role depends on the target service and the operations the application needs to perform.</p>
<p>From an infrastructure perspective, the principle is straightforward:</p>
<p><strong>Grant only the permissions required by the application.</strong></p>
<p>This follows the principle of least privilege and reduces unnecessary access across the Azure environment.</p>
<h2>8. Configure Ingress and Application Connectivity</h2>
<p>Once the application is deployed, users need a way to access it.</p>
<p>Azure Container Apps provides managed ingress capabilities, allowing applications to be exposed through HTTPS without manually managing an application gateway for every basic deployment scenario.</p>
<p>The infrastructure team needs to decide whether the application should be accessible through:</p>
<ul>
<li>External ingress – Accessible through a public application endpoint, subject to configured access controls.</li>
<li>Internal ingress – Accessible within the Container Apps Environment and its supported internal networking configuration.</li>
</ul>
<p>Before enabling ingress, validate the following:</p>
<ul>
<li>Is ingress enabled?</li>
<li>Should the application be internal or external?</li>
<li>Does the target port match the application listening port?</li>
<li>Is HTTPS configured correctly?</li>
<li>Does the application require additional authentication?</li>
<li>Are network restrictions required?</li>
<li>Are outbound connections to dependent services permitted?</li>
</ul>
<p>A common deployment issue is a healthy container that is not reachable because the application listening port and the Container Apps target port do not match.</p>
<p>For connectivity troubleshooting, validate the path in order:</p>
<img />
<p>This helps determine whether the issue is related to ingress, networking, container configuration or the application itself.</p>
<h2>9. Plan Scaling Before Production</h2>
<p>Getting one container running is only the first step.</p>
<p>The next question is:</p>
<p><strong>What happens when multiple users start accessing the application?</strong></p>
<p>Azure Container Apps supports replica-based scaling using configurable scaling rules, including HTTP traffic and other supported KEDA-based triggers.</p>
<p>Infrastructure teams should consider:</p>
<ul>
<li>Minimum replicas</li>
<li>Maximum replicas</li>
<li>CPU allocation</li>
<li>Memory allocation</li>
<li>Scaling triggers</li>
<li>Concurrent requests</li>
<li>Expected user traffic</li>
<li>Application startup time</li>
</ul>
<p>For an interactive application, maintaining a minimum replica count may be appropriate when avoiding cold-start latency is important.</p>
<p>However, AI applications introduce another important consideration.</p>
<p>The container application is not necessarily the bottleneck.</p>
<p>Azure OpenAI has its own model deployment capacity, quota and throttling considerations.</p>
<p>Therefore:</p>
<p><strong>Increasing Container Apps replicas does not automatically increase Azure OpenAI model capacity.</strong></p>
<p>Scaling decisions should consider two separate layers.</p>
<p><strong>Application capacity:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Container Apps replicas</li>
<li>CPU and memory</li>
<li>Request concurrency</li>
<li>Application-level performance</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>AI model capacity:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Azure OpenAI deployment capacity</li>
<li>Model quota</li>
<li>Token throughput</li>
<li>Request throttling</li>
<li>Retry and backoff behavior</li>
</ul>
<p>Load testing should be performed to establish appropriate limits rather than simply configuring a high maximum replica count.</p>
<h2>10. Consider Stateful Application Behaviour</h2>
<p>Interactive applications may maintain user or session state during execution.</p>
<p>This becomes particularly important when the application scales horizontally.</p>
<p>With a single replica, user interactions are handled by one running application instance.</p>
<p>With multiple replicas, requests may potentially be handled by different instances depending on the ingress and session configuration.</p>
<p>The infrastructure and application teams should establish one important detail:</p>
<p><strong>Is application state stored only inside the container, or is it persisted externally?</strong></p>
<p>If application or session state must survive container restarts, scaling events or deployments, an external persistence mechanism should be evaluated.</p>
<p>Container memory and local container storage should not be treated as durable application storage.</p>
<p>For Streamlit and similar interactive applications, the application team should also validate session handling and WebSocket connectivity under the expected ingress and scaling configuration.</p>
<p>This discussion should happen before increasing the application's replica count.</p>
<h2>11. Validate the Manual Deployment Before Automating It</h2>
<p>It can be tempting to start immediately with CI/CD pipelines.</p>
<p>However, from an infrastructure perspective, I prefer validating the complete deployment lifecycle manually before introducing automation.</p>
<p>The initial deployment should establish that the following process works:</p>
<img />
<p>Once this process is successful, the same steps can be automated through Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions.</p>
<p>The automated deployment lifecycle then becomes:</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>
<img />
<p>This approach makes troubleshooting easier because each deployment stage has already been validated independently.</p>
<p>The CI/CD pipeline simply automates a process that is known to work.</p>
<h2>12. Authenticate the CI/CD Pipeline Securely</h2>
<p>The deployment pipeline also needs access to Azure resources.</p>
<p>Pipeline authentication should receive the same security attention as application authentication.</p>
<p>Where supported, use <strong>Workload Identity Federation (OIDC)</strong> rather than maintaining long-lived client secrets in pipeline variables.</p>
<p>The authentication flow looks like this:</p>
<img />
<p>This avoids creating another permanent credential simply to automate deployment.</p>
<p>Pipeline permissions should also follow least privilege.</p>
<p>The deployment identity should have sufficient permissions to perform the required deployment operations without receiving unnecessary access to unrelated subscriptions or resources.</p>
<h2>13. Manage Application Releases Using Revisions</h2>
<p>Application deployment does not end with the first successful release.</p>
<p>There will be a version 2, version 3 and eventually another release that may need to be rolled back.</p>
<p>Azure Container Apps provides a revision-based deployment model.</p>
<p>A revision represents a version of the application configuration and container template.</p>
<p>For example:</p>
<img />
<p>Depending on the configured revision mode, the application can use single-revision or multiple-revision deployment.</p>
<p>Multiple-revision mode is particularly useful when implementing controlled traffic splitting, blue-green deployments or canary releases.</p>
<p>This allows infrastructure teams to validate a new application version before directing all production traffic to it.</p>
<p>Combined with traceable container image tags, revisions make it easier to answer a common operational question:</p>
<p><strong>Which application version is actually running?</strong></p>
<p>A rollback strategy should also be defined before production deployment.</p>
<h2>14. Monitoring and Operational Visibility</h2>
<p>A successful infrastructure deployment should not end with:</p>
<p>"The container is running."</p>
<p>Once users start accessing the application, the infrastructure team needs operational visibility.</p>
<p>At a minimum, consider monitoring the following:</p>
<div class="styles_lia-table-wrapper__h6Xo9 styles_table-responsive__MW0lN"><table border="1" style="border-width: 1px;"><tbody><tr><th>Monitoring area</th><th>What to validate</th></tr><tr><td>Container health</td><td>Replica readiness and container restarts</td></tr><tr><td>Application logs</td><td>Startup failures and application exceptions</td></tr><tr><td>HTTP metrics</td><td>Request volume, status codes and response latency</td></tr><tr><td>Resource utilization</td><td>CPU and memory consumption</td></tr><tr><td>Scaling</td><td>Replica count and scaling activity</td></tr><tr><td>Connectivity</td><td>Access to dependent Azure services</td></tr><tr><td>Azure OpenAI</td><td>Authentication errors, throttling and request failures</td></tr></tbody><colgroup><col style="width: 50.00%;" /><col style="width: 50.00%;" /></colgroup></table></div>
<p>Azure Monitor and Log Analytics can provide the operational visibility needed around the deployed workload.</p>
<p>A practical troubleshooting sequence is:</p>
<img />
<p>Following this sequence prevents infrastructure, application and downstream-service issues from being mixed together.</p>
<p>For production environments, configure diagnostic settings and appropriate alerts rather than relying only on manual log inspection.</p>
<h2>15. Common Deployment Issues and Troubleshooting</h2>
<p>Here are some common issues that infrastructure engineers may encounter during an Azure Container Apps deployment.</p>
<h3>Issue 1: Container Image Cannot Be Pulled</h3>
<p><strong>Possible causes:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Incorrect registry configuration</li>
<li>Incorrect image name or tag</li>
<li>Missing registry permissions</li>
<li>Managed Identity misconfiguration</li>
<li>Private registry connectivity issues</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>What to check:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Validate the complete image reference.</li>
<li>Confirm the image exists in ACR.</li>
<li>Check the Container App registry configuration.</li>
<li>Verify the required registry pull permissions.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Issue 2: Application Starts and Immediately Restarts</h3>
<p><strong>Possible causes:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Missing environment variables</li>
<li>Incorrect startup command</li>
<li>Missing application dependencies</li>
<li>Missing secrets</li>
<li>Insufficient CPU or memory</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>What to check:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Container console logs</li>
<li>Container Apps system logs</li>
<li>Application startup configuration</li>
<li>Environment variable references</li>
<li>Resource allocation</li>
</ul>
<h3>Issue 3: Application Is Deployed but Not Reachable</h3>
<p><strong>Possible causes:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Incorrect target port</li>
<li>Application listening only on localhost</li>
<li>Ingress disabled</li>
<li>Incorrect internal or external ingress configuration</li>
<li>Network restrictions</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>What to check:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Container Apps ingress configuration</li>
<li>Application listening port</li>
<li>Application binding address</li>
<li>Network connectivity</li>
<li>HTTPS endpoint</li>
</ul>
<h3>Issue 4: Azure OpenAI Returns Authentication Errors</h3>
<p><strong>Possible causes:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Managed Identity not enabled</li>
<li>Incorrect role assignment</li>
<li>Incorrect endpoint configuration</li>
<li>Unsupported authentication method</li>
<li>Missing application configuration</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>What to check:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Managed Identity assignment</li>
<li>Azure RBAC permissions</li>
<li>Azure OpenAI endpoint</li>
<li>Application authentication configuration</li>
</ul>
<h3>Issue 5: Azure OpenAI Returns HTTP 429 Responses</h3>
<p>Do not immediately assume that the Container App needs more replicas.</p>
<p>Investigate:</p>
<ul>
<li>Azure OpenAI deployment capacity</li>
<li>Model quota and throughput</li>
<li>Request frequency</li>
<li>Token consumption</li>
<li>Retry and exponential backoff configuration</li>
</ul>
<p>The important distinction is:</p>
<p><strong>Container scaling and AI model capacity are two different things.</strong></p>
<h2>Final Thoughts</h2>
<p>Deploying an AI application is about much more than getting a container to start.</p>
<p>From an infrastructure perspective, the complete lifecycle involves packaging, registry management, identity, deployment, security, scaling, automation and monitoring.</p>
<p>Azure Container Apps provides a managed container platform that allows infrastructure teams to focus on these operational responsibilities without having to manage the underlying Kubernetes infrastructure.</p>
<p>For a Streamlit-based AI application, a practical implementation approach is to start small:</p>
<p><strong>Get one container running securely → Configure Managed Identity → Validate secrets and connectivity → Configure ingress → Test scaling → Automate deployment → Implement production monitoring.</strong></p>
<p>This incremental approach keeps application and infrastructure responsibilities clear and makes troubleshooting considerably easier.</p>
<p>The goal is not simply to get an AI application running.</p>
<p>The goal is to make the deployment:</p>
<p><strong>Secure. Repeatable. Observable. Scalable. Production-ready.</strong></p>
</details>

## Azure Networking Blog

### Redefining Application Load Balancing in Azure Application Gateway

- **Link**: [https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/azure-networking-blog/redefining-application-load-balancing-in-azure-application/ba-p/4572687](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/azure-networking-blog/redefining-application-load-balancing-in-azure-application/ba-p/4572687)
- **Published**: 2026-11-12 16:29:59
- **Fetched**: 2026-11-12 22:22:31

<details class="entry-summary">
<summary>詳細を表示</summary>
<p><em>By Jay Soni (Senior Product Manager) and Jordi Rey (Product Manager), Azure Application Gateway</em></p>
<p style="text-align: center;"><img alt="Advanced routing rules and advanced load balancing in Azure Application Gateway" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," width="800" /></p>
<p>Modern applications change quickly. Teams run A/B experiments, version their APIs, tailor experiences by client and tenant, and serve AI models across reserved and pay-as-you-go capacity. Azure Application Gateway now gives you more precise control over where each request goes and how traffic is distributed once it gets there.</p>
<p>Two new capabilities are now in public preview. Use them on their own or together:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Advanced routing rules:</strong> Match requests on path, header, query string, HTTP method and client IP, with regular expression support. A single rule can now cover request patterns that previously needed several.</li>
<li><strong>Advanced load balancing:</strong> Choose backend pools by weight or priority, then choose servers within each pool using round robin, weighted round robin or least connections.</li>
</ul>
<p>The rest of this post explains how these capabilities work and the scenarios they enable, from blue-green deployments and client-aware experiences to multi-tenant SaaS and a single entry point for your AI endpoints.</p>
<h2>What's new</h2>
<div class="styles_lia-table-wrapper__h6Xo9 styles_table-responsive__MW0lN"><table border="1" style="width: 100%; border-width: 1px;"><thead><tr><th>Capability</th><th>Details</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>What a rule can match</td><td>Path, HTTP header, query string, HTTP method and client IP</td></tr><tr><td>How values are matched</td><td>Exact values, or RE2 regular expressions for path, header and query string</td></tr><tr><td>How conditions combine</td><td>Up to five conditions per rule, joined with AND and evaluated in priority order</td></tr><tr><td>Load balancing across pools</td><td>Multiple pools per rule, selected by weight or by priority</td></tr><tr><td>Load balancing within a pool</td><td>Round robin, weighted round robin or least connections, set per pool</td></tr><tr><td>Failover between pools</td><td>Priority-based failover driven by a configurable Minimum Healthy Percent</td></tr></tbody><colgroup><col style="width: 50.00%;" /><col style="width: 50.00%;" /></colgroup></table></div>
<h2>Advanced routing rules: more control over request routing</h2>
<p>Define conditions on URL paths, HTTP headers, query strings, HTTP methods and client IP addresses to send each request to the right backend pool. Combine conditions in one rule to support scenarios such as API versioning, tenant-specific routing and feature-based deployments. Rules are evaluated in priority order, and the first matching rule determines the destination. Requests that don't match any rule go to the configured default backend pool.</p>
<p>Path, header and query-string conditions support RE2 regular expressions, so a single pattern can match many request variations. For example, <code>^/api/orders(/.*)?$</code> matches <code>/api/orders</code> and all of its subpaths. Each rule can also apply a rewrite rule set as part of routing.</p>
<h2>Advanced load balancing: traffic distribution that fits your workload</h2>
<p>Advanced load balancing gives you control at two levels:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Across pools:</strong> Use weighted distribution to split traffic by relative weight, such as 80/20 for a gradual rollout. Or use priority to keep traffic on a primary pool and fail over to the next pool when the primary pool's healthy servers drop below your Minimum Healthy Percent.</li>
<li><strong>Within a pool:</strong> Each pool uses its own algorithm. Round robin spreads requests evenly. Weighted round robin sends more requests to larger servers. Least connections sends each request to the healthy server with the fewest active connections, so a server still working through long-running requests receives less new traffic.</li>
</ul>
<p style="text-align: center;"><img alt="Figure 1: Advanced routing rules match the request; advanced load balancing selects a pool by weight or priority, then a server within the pool" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," width="800" /></p>
<p><em>Figure 1. Advanced routing rules match the request. Advanced load balancing then selects a pool by weight or priority, and a server within that pool.</em></p>
<h2>Scenarios you can build</h2>
<h3>Canary and blue-green releases</h3>
<p>Route requests that carry an <code>x-release: canary</code> header to a new version, or send 10% of all traffic to the green pool and raise its weight as confidence grows. Taking a pool out of rotation is a weight change, not a redeployment, and your customer-facing endpoint never changes.</p>
<h3>Read/write split</h3>
<p>Send GET requests to a pool of read replicas or cache-heavy nodes, and send POST, PUT and DELETE requests to the primary write tier.</p>
<h3>Client-aware experiences</h3>
<p>Route mobile clients to an optimized backend based on a client header such as <code>x-client-type: mobile</code> or a User-Agent pattern, while web traffic continues to the standard pool.</p>
<h3>Internal and partner traffic</h3>
<p>Route requests from corporate or partner IP ranges to dedicated backend pools, such as staging or administrative environments. Combine client IP-based routing with Web Application Firewall (WAF) protection and appropriate authentication and authorization controls to help secure access to these applications.</p>
<h3>Multi-tenant SaaS</h3>
<p>Route by tenant hostname to dedicated pools for premium tenants and shared pools for everyone else. Tenant tiers become a routing decision, not an infrastructure redesign.</p>
<h3>API versioning without URL changes</h3>
<p>Route <code>?api-version=2026-01</code> or an <code>api-version</code> header to the right backend. Clients keep a stable URL while you run several versions side by side, and one regular expression condition can cover a whole family of versioned paths.</p>
<h2>One entry point for your AI endpoints</h2>
<p>AI applications often span several endpoints, mixing reserved Provisioned Throughput Unit (PTU) capacity and pay-as-you-go capacity across regions. Rather than having every application track which endpoint to call and what to do when reserved capacity runs out, Application Gateway can serve as the central entry point for all of them: one address, with TLS, WAF and private connectivity managed in one place.</p>
<p><strong>Route by deployment, spill over automatically.</strong> Route AI requests to the appropriate backend pools based on deployment paths, team identifiers or application-specific headers. Put PTU endpoints in a priority 1 pool and pay-as-you-go endpoints in a priority 2 pool. Traffic moves to pay-as-you-go only when the share of healthy reserved endpoints drops below your Minimum Healthy Percent, with no change for the client.</p>
<p style="text-align: center;"><img alt="Figure 2: Application Gateway as one entry point for AI endpoints with priority failover from PTU to pay-as-you-go" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," width="800" /></p>
<p><em>Figure 2. One entry point for your AI endpoints: route by deployment path or header, and fail over by priority.</em></p>
<h2>Get started</h2>
<p>Advanced routing rules and advanced load balancing are available for both new and existing Application Gateway deployments. To get started, see the <a href="https://aka.ms/appgw/advancedloadbalancing" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Application Gateway documentation for advanced routing rules and advanced load balancing</a>.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> Requires API version 2026-03-01 or later. During preview, weighted distribution doesn't check pool health, so set a pool's weight to 0 to take it out of rotation.</p>
<p><em>This feature is in public preview. Previews are provided without a service-level agreement and aren't recommended for production workloads. For more information, see the <a href="https://azure.microsoft.com/support/legal/preview-supplemental-terms/" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Supplemental Terms of Use for Microsoft Azure Previews</a>.</em></p>
</details>

## Apps on Azure Blog

### Python support has arrived in the guided Copilot experience for VS Code

- **Link**: [https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/apps-on-azure-blog/python-support-has-arrived-in-the-guided-copilot-experience-for/ba-p/4572591](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/apps-on-azure-blog/python-support-has-arrived-in-the-guided-copilot-experience-for/ba-p/4572591)
- **Published**: 2026-11-12 01:56:47
- **Fetched**: 2026-11-12 13:34:40

<details class="entry-summary">
<summary>詳細を表示</summary>
<p>When we introduced the&nbsp;<a href="https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/AppsonAzureBlog/introducing-a-guided-copilot-experience-for-building-azure-apps-in-vs-code/4557120" rel="noopener" target="_blank">guided Copilot experience for building Azure apps in VS Code</a>, we started with JavaScript and TypeScript, with Python on the roadmap. Since then, we've seen people creating Python projects with the experience, and we wanted to make sure our Python lovers had proper support.</p>
<p>Today, we're excited to announce that the guided Copilot experience in VS Code now fully supports Python projects. 🐍</p>
<h2>From Python idea to Azure app</h2>
<p>The guided experience helps you move from an idea to a deployed Azure app through a structured workflow, with checkpoints for reviewing important decisions. Now Python developers can use that same experience to:</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>
<img />
<p>&nbsp;</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Plan and scaffold:</strong> Describe your app, review the proposed architecture, and approve a plan before code is generated.</li>
<li><strong>Develop locally:</strong> Get help preparing your development environment, then run and iterate on your Python project in VS Code.</li>
<li><strong>Deploy to Azure:</strong> Review the deployment tools, resources, and estimated costs before deploying your app.</li>
</ol>
<p>This guided path complements the free-form Copilot workflows you already know, so you can choose the approach that works best for you.</p>
<h2>Give it a try</h2>
<p>Install the <a href="https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-vscode.vscode-node-azure-pack" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Azure Tools extension pack</a>, open an empty folder in VS Code, and start the guided Copilot experience with your Python project in mind.</p>
<p>Whether you're building an API, prototyping an idea, or learning something new, we'd love to see what you create. Have feedback? <a href="https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-azureresourcegroups/" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Share it with us on GitHub</a>.</p>
<p>Thanks to everyone who's been building Python projects with the experience. We're excited to see what you make next!</p>
</details>

### Introducing Azure Container Apps as a target workload in Azure Migrate

- **Link**: [https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/apps-on-azure-blog/introducing-azure-container-apps-as-a-target-workload-in-azure/ba-p/4571669](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/apps-on-azure-blog/introducing-azure-container-apps-as-a-target-workload-in-azure/ba-p/4571669)
- **Published**: 2026-11-12 14:51:04
- **Fetched**: 2026-11-12 22:22:32

<details class="entry-summary">
<summary>詳細を表示</summary>
<p>We are excited to announce <strong>Azure Container Apps as a target workload for assessment in Azure Migrate</strong>, helping organizations evaluate existing web applications for migration to a managed, serverless container platform.</p>
<p>This capability extends the Azure Migrate assessment experience to Azure Container Apps, bringing application readiness, migration requirements, sizing recommendations, and estimated hosting costs into migration planning. Organizations can identify suitable applications, understand the changes required, and make informed decisions before starting migration.</p>
<p>Supported workloads include Web Apps discovered through Azure Migrate</p>
<h2>Make informed modernization and migration decisions</h2>
<p>For organizations with an existing application estate, modernization starts with a few essential questions: Which applications are suitable for container-based hosting? What needs to change? What resources will they require, and what will they cost to run?</p>
<p>Azure Migrate helps answer these questions through discovery and assessment. With Azure Container Apps as a workload target, migration teams can:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Assess application readiness:</strong> Evaluate existing web applications for migration to Azure Container Apps.</li>
<li><strong>Identify migration requirements:</strong> Review compatibility issues, warnings, and recommended remediation.</li>
<li><strong>Review resource recommendations:</strong> Understand the compute requirements of the assessed applications.</li>
<li><strong>Estimate hosting costs:</strong> Use assessment estimates to support migration decisions and budgeting.</li>
<li><strong>Plan migration waves:</strong> Turn assessment insights into manageable migration batches.</li>
</ul>
<p>These insights help migration teams and application owners establish a shared understanding of migration scope, effort, and priorities.</p>
<h2>Why Azure Container Apps?</h2>
<p>Azure Container Apps enables organizations to run containerized applications without managing servers or the underlying container orchestration infrastructure.</p>
<p>The platform supports web applications, APIs, microservices, and background processing, with capabilities including:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Automatic scaling</strong> based on HTTP traffic or event-driven rules, including scale-to-zero for supported configurations.</li>
<li><strong>Managed ingress</strong> for application endpoints.</li>
<li><strong>Application revisions and traffic splitting</strong> to support controlled updates.</li>
<li><strong>Connectivity to dependent services</strong>, including databases, storage, and messaging.</li>
</ul>
<p>Adding Azure Container Apps as an assessment target helps organizations evaluate these capabilities against the requirements of existing applications before migration begins.</p>
<h2>From discovery to migration</h2>
<h3>1. Discover existing web applications</h3>
<p>Start with an Azure Migrate project and configure the Azure Migrate appliance for the source environment.</p>
<p>Discovery builds an inventory of web applications and their hosting servers. Review the discovered applications and dependency information to establish the assessment scope.</p>
<img />
<p class="lia-clear-both">&nbsp;</p>
<p><em>Review discovered web applications and select workloads for assessment. The inventory includes discovered workloads; discovery alone does not establish readiness for Azure Container Apps.</em></p>
<h3>2. Assess for Azure Container Apps</h3>
<p>Create a web app assessment for the selected applications and choose Azure Container Apps as the target.</p>
<p>Configure the applicable assessment settings, including target region and sizing preferences, then run the assessment to generate readiness findings, resource recommendations, and estimated costs.</p>
<img />
<p class="lia-clear-both">&nbsp;</p>
<p><em>Create an assessment for the discovered web app workloads.</em></p>
<h3>3. Review results and decide</h3>
<p>Review the assessment findings to understand which applications are ready for migration and which require changes.</p>
<p>Evaluate migration issues alongside business criticality, application dependencies, and operational requirements. Use these insights to select applications for migration and prioritize modernization work.</p>
<img />
<p>&nbsp;</p>
<p>Navigate to the <em>Azure Container Apps</em> tab for more details on the readiness</p>
<img />
<p><em>Review readiness and estimated monthly costs for Azure Container Apps. This example shows three web apps ready for migration and one not ready, with a cost estimate for the three ready apps. Estimates vary by workload and assessment settings.</em></p>
<h3>4. Plan migration waves</h3>
<p>After selecting the migration path, use <strong>Azure Migrate wave planning</strong>, to organize assessed applications and workloads into migration batches.</p>
<p>Review the proposed waves, sequencing, dependencies, and risks. Refine assignments with application owners and stakeholders, then commit approved waves.</p>
<p>Committing a wave accepts the migration plan; it does not start migration. The approved scope and assessment findings provide the foundation for application preparation and deployment.</p>
<h3>5. Migrate to Azure Container Apps</h3>
<p>Continue the approved migration plan in <a class="lia-external-url" href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/developer/github-copilot-app-modernization/overview" rel="noopener" target="_blank">GitHub Copilot app modernization</a>, using the Azure Migrate assessment findings, application scope, and dependency information as context. The tooling handles application code changes, validation, containerization, and deployment to Azure Container Apps.</p>
<p>Follow the workflow for the application's language:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Java:</strong> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-apps/migrate-java-github-copilot-app-modernization" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Migrate with GitHub Copilot app modernization</a>, including <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-apps/migrate-java-github-copilot-app-modernization#containerize-your-application" rel="noopener" target="_blank">containerization</a> and <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-apps/migrate-java-github-copilot-app-modernization#deploy-to-azure-container-apps" rel="noopener" target="_blank">deployment to Azure Container Apps</a>.</li>
<li><strong>.NET:</strong> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/azure/migration/appmod/overview" rel="noopener" target="_blank">GitHub Copilot modernization overview</a> and <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/azure/migration/appmod/deploy" rel="noopener" target="_blank">deployment workflow</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Get started</h2>
<p>Assess existing web applications for Azure Container Apps and move forward with a migration grounded in application readiness, resource requirements, and cost insights.</p>
<p>Explore the resources:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/migrate/migrate-services-overview" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Azure Migrate overview</a></li>
<li><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-apps/overview" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Azure Container Apps overview</a></li>
<li><a class="lia-external-url" href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-apps/migrate-azure-migrate" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Migrate to Azure Container Apps with Azure Migrate</a></li>
<li><a class="lia-external-url" href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/migrate/tutorial-app-containerization-java-container-apps?view=migrate" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Containerize Java Web Apps and Migrate to Azure Container Apps - Azure Migrate</a></li>
</ul>
</details>
